newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr manoeuvres in very familiar space.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr manoeuvres in very familiar space.

text.p: The Australian dollar idled through another indecisive session on Friday to notch up its 23rd consecutive trading day in the US$0.7720/7860 range.
Support was provided by exporter and Chinese bank bids and by a modest pullback in the yen which saw US$/yen rally more than 1-1/2 big figures from a deep low of 114.65 offshore.

Sentiment was also bolstered by strength in certain key commodity prices, particularly copper, which saw the influential CRB index to a one year high. Dealers, however, said the local market could not shake its bearish short term attitude and customers were keener to sell rallies than buy dips.

By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar was keeping a low profile at US$0.7750/55 from an early US$0.7763/68 and US$0.7762/67 late here Thursday. Support was put at US$0.7750 but US$0.7720 remained the key bulwark after it absorbed heavy punishment on Thursday, while dealers expected fresh offers atop US$0.7780.
The upside was also thick with chart resistance after more than a month of choppy trading with US$09.7805, US$0.7835 and US$0.7860 all worthy of respect.
On the crosses the currency managed a meagre bounce to 90.50/60 yen from 90.13/23 late Thursday, in line with the U.S. dollar which made it to 116.55/65 from 115.75/85 in New York.

Recent market concerns about a possible rise in Japanese interest rates eased a touch when the Bank of Japan said the emphasis for monetary policy would remain to make the recovery firmer and the Ministry of Finance sadi the low rate policy was contributing to stabilising prices.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Rubin also went a little way to countering rumours the U.S. wanted to see US$/yen at 115.00 by reiterrating his support for a strong dollar, saying it helped keep inflation down.
The U.S. currency had struggled back to 116.40/50 yen late here Friday after diving as low as 114.70 Thursday.
The suppressant effect of a firm US$ might be needed given core consumer price inflation, reported Thursday, rose a higher than expected 0.3 percent in April.

The figures added some more weight to the case for a rate hike by the Federal Reserve, but the market remains deeply divided on whether the central bank will tighen at its next policy meeting on May 20.

A hike would be bearish for the A$ short term since it would narrow the interest differential between the currencies. In the longer term, however, it could be argued the U.S. economic strength the rate hike reflected, was bullish for the A$.

A sustained period of above trend U.S. growth would tend to underpin emerging recoveries in Japan and Europe and eventually lead to synchronised world pick-up, analysts reckoned. That in turn could be expected to support the price of commodities, Australia's largest export earner.
The outlook for U.S. monetary policy remained a major uncertainty for both dollars, with the market split on whether the Federal Reserve would tighten at its meeting next Tuesday.
Implications for the A$ were mixed since the lack of a hike would keep its yield advantage intact but was also likely to see US$/yen slide which would tend to drag it down on the crosses.

Interest differentials were clearly important in the short term, however, as shown by the Canadian dollar which leapt today after the Bank of Canada switched to a neutral policy stance from the highly stimulative position held in the past few years.

The A$ dived as a result to C$1.0618/29 from C$1.0776/86 Thursday and traders wondered if offshore investors might now think about switching into the CAD as a commodity currency with the potential for higher interest rates.
In contrast the risk here was still for an easing and key domestic wages data on Thursdsay could yet decide if the RBA cut again. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
